They combat inflammation by displacing pro-inflammatory fats, producing anti-inflammatory molecules, and inhibiting inflammatory gene expression. To improve sleep, ensure your mattress is medium-firm with good support, replace it every 7–10 years, and use pillows for spinal alignment. Sleep in a cool room (16–18°C), maintain a consistent sleep schedule, and create a calm wind-down routine. Avoid caffeine after 2 pm and time pain relief before bed.

Losing 1kg of body weight can reduce knee joint loading by 4kg during walking. A 5-10% reduction in body weight over 3-6 months is an achievable goal, with sustainable weight loss of 0.5-1kg per week being recommended.

/blog/arthritis-fatigue-management-uk.question: Managing Arthritis Fatigue – A UK Guide
/blog/arthritis-fatigue-management-uk.answer: Arthritis fatigue is an overwhelming exhaustion not fully relieved by rest, affecting concentration, mood, and motivation. It differs from normal tiredness and can be as debilitating as pain. Inflammation, pain, poor sleep, anaemia, specific medications, reduced fitness, and the emotional burden of chronic illness all contribute to this profound fatigue. Energy management techniques like prioritising, planning, pacing, positioning, and self-permission can help.

faqs.q: What Is Arthritis Fatigue?
faqs.a: Arthritis fatigue is different from normal tiredness. It's an overwhelming, whole-body exhaustion that: Doesn't improve fully with rest or sleep Can be as debilitating as the pain itself Affects concentration, mood, and motivation Can strike suddenly or build throughout the day Makes simple tasks feel overwhelmingly difficult

faqs.q: Why Does Arthritis Cause Fatigue?
faqs.a: Inflammation — cytokines released during inflammation directly cause fatigue Pain — chronic pain is mentally and physically exhausting Poor sleep — pain disrupts sleep quality, even if you sleep long hours Anaemia — common in inflammatory arthritis, reducing oxygen delivery Medications — some arthritis drugs cause fatigue as a side effect Reduced fitness — deconditioning from reduced activity Emotional burden — living with chronic illness is emotionally draining

/blog/back-arthritis-exercises-uk.question: Best Exercises for Back Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiothera
/blog/back-arthritis-exercises-uk.answer: Exercise is a core treatment for back arthritis, offering significant pain reduction comparable to medication. faqs.q: What are the best exercises for an arthritic back?
faqs.a: The best routine combines deep-core strengthening (pelvic tilts, bird-dog, glute bridges), spinal mobility (cat-cow, knee-to-chest) and low-impact aerobic work (walking, cycling, swimming). Done 3–4 times per week, this can reduce back pain by 25–40%.

faqs.q: How often should I do back exercises for arthritis?
faqs.a: Strengthening 2–3 times per week, mobility daily (5–10 minutes), aerobic 3–5 times per week (30 minutes, can be split into 3 × 10 min).

faqs.q: Can exercise cure back arthritis?
faqs.a: No, but it is the most effective non-surgical treatment for spinal OA and can delay or avoid the need for spinal injections or surgery. Benefits stop if exercise stops.

faqs.q: What exercises should I avoid with back arthritis?
faqs.a: Avoid heavy deadlifts, loaded sit-ups, high-impact running with severe OA and unsupported overhead pressing. Stick to partial squats, bird-dog and stationary cycling.

faqs.q: Are there gentle back exercises for severe arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes — pelvic tilts, supported knee-to-chest, cat-cow, pool walking and stationary cycling on low resistance. Two short 10-minute daily sessions are usually better tolerated.

faqs.q: How long until back exercises reduce arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Reduced stiffness within 2–3 weeks, meaningful pain reduction at 6–8 weeks, full benefit at 12 weeks of consistent practice.

/blog/knee-arthritis-exercises-uk.question: Best Exercises for Knee Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiothera
/blog/knee-arthritis-exercises-uk.answer: Regular exercise is crucial for managing knee arthritis, reducing pain by 25–50% on average, strengthening supporting muscles, and improving flexibility. A balanced programme includes strengthening exercises (2-3 times/week), such as straight leg raises and wall sits, alongside flexibility exercises daily and 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly, like walking or swimming. Controlled joint loading helps nourish cartilage without worsening arthritis.

faqs.q: What are the best exercises for arthritic knees?
faqs.a: The best exercises for arthritic knees combine three elements: strengthening (straight leg raises, sit-to-stand, wall sits and step-ups), low-impact aerobic work (stationary cycling, swimming or brisk walking) and daily flexibility (heel slides, hamstring stretches and calf stretches). Done 3–4 times per week, this combination reduces knee pain by 25–50% on average — comparable to the effect of paracetamol or NSAIDs.

faqs.q: How often should I do knee exercises for arthritis?
faqs.a: UK physiotherapy guidance recommends strengthening exercises 2–3 times per week, low-impact aerobic exercise 3–5 times per week (30 minutes per session, which can be split into 3 × 10 minutes) and gentle range-of-motion stretches every day. Allow at least one rest day between strengthening sessions to let muscle recover.

faqs.q: Can exercise cure knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Exercise cannot reverse cartilage loss or cure knee arthritis, but it is the single most effective non-surgical treatment. A consistent 12-week programme can reduce pain by 25–50%, improve walking distance, delay the need for joint replacement and improve quality of life. The benefits stop if exercise stops — it is a long-term management tool, not a short course.

faqs.q: What exercises should I avoid with knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Avoid high-impact activities (running on concrete, jumping, plyometrics), deep squats below 90°, heavy seated leg-extension machines, and lunges where the front knee travels well beyond the toes. Replace them with stationary cycling, swimming, sit-to-stand from a chair, and partial squats to a chair height.

faqs.q: Are there low-impact knee exercises for severe arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. Seated knee extensions, heel slides, isometric quad sets, ankle pumps and warm-water (hydrotherapy) exercise are all suitable for severe knee arthritis. Two short 10-minute sessions per day are usually better tolerated than one longer session, and there is no requirement to weight-bear for the exercises to be effective.

faqs.q: How long does it take for knee exercises to reduce arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Most people notice reduced stiffness within 2–3 weeks of consistent practice. Meaningful pain reduction typically appears at 6–8 weeks, with the full benefit of a structured programme seen at 12 weeks. Stopping for more than 2–3 weeks usually reverses the gains.

/blog/osteoarthritis-symptoms-uk.answer: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, affecting millions. It occurs when cartilage cushioning bone ends wears down. Symptoms develop slowly and include joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and reduced movement. Common affected joints are the knees, hips, hands, lower back, and neck. See a GP if symptoms persist for weeks, worsen, or affect daily activities.

faqs.q: What are the best exercises for arthritic shoulders?
faqs.a: The best routine combines pendulum swings and wall slides (mobility), band external rotation and scapular squeezes (strength), and warm-up with a heat pack for 10 minutes. Done 3–4 times per week, this combination reduces pain and improves overhead reach.

faqs.q: How often should I do shoulder exercises for arthritis?
faqs.a: Mobility daily (5–10 minutes), strengthening 2–3 times per week. Allow at least one rest day between strengthening sessions.

faqs.q: Can exercise cure shoulder arthritis?
faqs.a: No — exercise cannot reverse cartilage loss, but it is the most effective non-surgical treatment and can delay the need for shoulder replacement. Benefits stop if exercise stops.

faqs.q: What shoulder exercises should I avoid with arthritis?
faqs.a: Avoid behind-the-neck lat pulldowns, military presses, upright rows and heavy overhead lifting. Replace with band external rotation, wall push-ups and seated rows.

faqs.q: Are there gentle shoulder exercises for severe arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes — pendulum swings, supported table slides, scapular squeezes and warm-water exercise. Two short 10-minute daily sessions are usually better tolerated.

faqs.q: How long until shoulder exercises reduce arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Reduced stiffness within 2–3 weeks, meaningful pain reduction at 6–8 weeks, full benefit at 12 weeks of consistent practice.

faqs.q: Can stress cause my arthritis to flare up after a period of calm?
faqs.a: Yes, stress is a known trigger for arthritis flares in many people. Emotional or physical stress can impact your immune system and inflammatory pathways, potentially making your symptoms return or worsen even when you've been well.

faqs.q: How long does a typical arthritis flare last if I've stopped treatment?
faqs.a: The duration of a flare varies greatly among individuals and types of arthritis. Without treatment, flares can last for weeks or even months, often becoming more severe and potentially leading to joint damage over time.

faqs.q: Is it possible to restart my old medication if my symptoms come back?
faqs.a: Often, yes – if a medication worked for you before, your clinician might suggest restarting it. However, they will review your current situation thoroughly as your health needs or the effectiveness of certain drugs can change over time.

faqs.q: Is gene therapy currently available for arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: No, gene therapy for common forms of arthritis is not currently a standard treatment option available in the UK. Research is ongoing, but these approaches are still considered experimental and are not part of routine clinical care.

faqs.q: How does gene therapy for arthritis typically work in theory?
faqs.a: In theory, gene therapy aims to introduce new genetic material into cells to either produce beneficial proteins (like anti-inflammatory molecules or cartilage-repairing factors) or to block the production of harmful ones that contribute to arthritis. The goal is to modify the disease process at a cellular level.

faqs.q: Will gene therapy replace existing arthritis treatments in the future?
faqs.a: It's too early to say if gene therapy will replace existing treatments. If successful, it's more likely to become another tool in the treatment toolkit, possibly used in specific types of arthritis or for people who haven't responded well to current therapies. It would likely complement rather than entirely replace established approaches.

faqs.q: What kind of adaptations can these grants cover?
faqs.a: Grants can cover a wide range of adaptations, from minor adjustments like grab rails and ramps to larger works such as accessible showers, stairlifts, widening doorways, or even extensions for downstairs facilities. The specific adaptations approved will depend on your individual needs and the grant's criteria.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay the grant back?
faqs.a: No, Disabled Facilities Grants are typically non-repayable, provided that the conditions of the grant are met and the work is completed as approved. However, some local council schemes might be structured as loans or have specific terms around repayment or charges if the property is sold within a certain timeframe.

faqs.q: Can I apply if I live in rented accommodation?
faqs.a: Yes, you can apply for grants if you live in rented accommodation. However, you will need to get permission from your landlord before any adaptations can be made to the property. It's often a good idea to discuss this with your landlord at an early stage.

/blog/managing-methotrexate-side-effects.question: Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips
/blog/managing-methotrexate-side-effects.answer: Common methotrexate side effects like nausea, fatigue, and mouth ulcers are often manageable. Taking prescribed folic acid significantly reduces these. If you experience new or concerning symptoms, such as sudden joint pain, fever, yellowing skin, or persistent vomiting, contact your doctor. Never stop methotrexate suddenly without consulting your care team due to the risk of disease flares.

faqs.q: Can my diet help with methotrexate side effects?
faqs.a: While no specific diet cures side effects, a balanced and nutritious diet can support your overall health and energy levels. Some people find that avoiding certain foods, like highly processed items, helps with nausea, but this is often very individual.

faqs.q: How do I manage fatigue from methotrexate?
faqs.a: Managing fatigue often involves a combination of strategies: ensuring you get enough rest, pacing your activities, and staying gently active. Discussing your fatigue with your care team is important as they may suggest adjustments to your medication schedule or recommend additional support.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink alcohol while taking methotrexate?
faqs.a: It's generally advised to limit or avoid alcohol completely while taking methotrexate due to the potential for liver impact. Always discuss alcohol consumption with your doctor, as they can provide personalised advice based on your health and the specifics of your treatment.

faqs.q: What does DAS28 mean?
faqs.a: DAS28 stands for "Disease Activity Score in 28 joints." It's a tool used by rheumatologists to measure how active your rheumatoid arthritis is. It takes into account the number of tender and swollen joints, your general health assessment, and a blood test result (ESR or CRP) to give a single score.

faqs.q: Can I travel if I'm on a biologic?
faqs.a: Generally, yes, but it's important to plan ahead. You might need a letter from your doctor for airport security regarding needles or temperature-sensitive medication. Discuss any travel plans, especially to areas with higher infection risk, with your rheumatology team well in advance.

faqs.q: How often will I have injections?
faqs.a: The frequency of injections depends on the specific biologic medication you are prescribed. Some biologics are given weekly, others every two weeks, or even monthly. Your rheumatology team will explain your specific dosing schedule and show you how to administer the injection if it's self-administered.

/blog/nsaid-stomach-protection-when-you-.question: NSAID Stomach Protection: When You Need a PPI
/blog/nsaid-stomach-protection-when-you-.answer: Combining a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) like omeprazole with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) significantly reduces the risk of gastrointestinal side effects including stomach ulcers and bleeding. This co-prescription is recommended for individuals at increased risk, such as those with a history of stomach problems, older adults, and those taking blood-thinning medications. PPIs offer vital protection when taking NSAIDs long-term or at higher doses.
/blog/nsaid-stomach-protection-when-you-.breadcrumb: NSAID Stomach Protection: When You Need a PPI

faqs.q: Can I stop taking my PPI if I no longer take NSAIDs?
faqs.a: It is generally safe to stop your PPI once you stop taking NSAIDs, unless your doctor has prescribed it for another condition. Always discuss this with your doctor first to ensure it's appropriate for your individual health situation.

faqs.q: Are there any long-term side effects of taking omeprazole?
faqs.a: Most people tolerate omeprazole well, but long-term use can sometimes be associated with certain issues like nutrient deficiencies or an increased risk of specific infections. Your doctor will weigh these potential risks against the benefits of preventing serious stomach complications.

faqs.q: What if I forget to take my omeprazole dose?
faqs.a: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it's almost time for your next dose, skip the missed one and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a forgotten one.

/blog/nsaids-and-arthritis-benefits-risk.question: NSAIDs and Arthritis: Benefits, Risks and Safer Use
/blog/nsaids-and-arthritis-benefits-risk.answer: NSAIDs effectively reduce arthritis pain and stiffness, with benefits often appearing within hours to days, though responses vary. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, as side effects on the digestive system and kidneys become more likely with higher doses and longer-term use. Topical NSAIDs may offer localised relief with fewer systemic side effects.
/blog/nsaids-and-arthritis-benefits-risk.breadcrumb: NSAIDs and Arthritis: Benefits, Risks and Safer Use

faqs.q: Can I take NSAIDs every day for my arthritis?
faqs.a: Daily use of NSAIDs for arthritis should always be discussed with a doctor. While some people may need them regularly, it's generally advised to use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time possible due to potential side effects with long-term use.

faqs.q: Are topical NSAIDs safer than oral NSAIDs?
faqs.a: Topical NSAIDs (gels, creams) are often considered safer than oral forms because less of the medication is absorbed into your bloodstream. This means they carry a lower risk of digestive or kidney side effects, making them a good option for localised joint pain.

faqs.q: What should I do if NSAIDs don't help my pain?
faqs.a: If NSAIDs aren't effectively managing your pain, it's important to speak to your doctor or a healthcare professional. They can review your diagnosis, adjust your treatment plan, or explore other pain relief options that might be more suitable for you.

/blog/oa-vs-ra-comparison.question: Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis — Understanding the Differences
/blog/oa-vs-ra-comparison.answer: Osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) both cause joint pain but differ fundamentally. OA involves cartilage breakdown, usually from wear and tear, and commonly affects knees, hips, and hands. RA is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks joint linings, causing inflammation and damage — typically symmetrical, often starting in smaller joints on both sides of the body.

faqs.q: What Is Osteoarthritis (OA)?
faqs.a: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK, affecting around 8.75 million people . It is sometimes called "wear-and-tear" arthritis, though that phrase oversimplifies things. The smooth cartilage that cushions the ends of your bones gradually breaks down. Over time, the joint space narrows, bone rubs on bone, and the joint itself may change shape. Small bony growths called osteophytes (bone spurs) may form. faqs.q: What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)?
faqs.a: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease . The body's immune system — which normally fights infection — mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints (the synovium). This causes inflammation, swelling, and eventually joint damage. RA affects around 430,000 people in the UK. It is less common than OA but generally more aggressive. faqs.q: Can You Have Both OA and RA?
faqs.a: Yes, it is possible to have both. In fact, this is not uncommon. Someone with long-standing RA may develop secondary OA in the affected joints because of the damage caused by inflammation over time. Diagnosis and treatment of dual conditions require careful management by your rheumatology team.

faqs.q: Can I take paracetamol with other arthritis medications?
faqs.a: Generally, yes, but it's crucial to check with your doctor or pharmacist. They can advise on potential interactions with your specific medications, especially other pain relievers or anti-inflammatory drugs.

faqs.q: How long does paracetamol take to work for arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Paracetamol typically starts to relieve pain within 30 to 60 minutes after taking it. The effect usually lasts for a few hours. If you don't feel any benefit within this time, speak to your clinician.

faqs.q: Is long-term use of paracetamol safe for arthritis?
faqs.a: While paracetamol is considered safe for many when taken correctly, long-term daily use should always be discussed with a healthcare professional. They can monitor for any potential side effects and ensure it remains the most appropriate treatment for your pain.

faqs.q: How can I make lifting my child easier with sore joints?
faqs.a: Focus on using your larger muscle groups, like your legs, rather than your back or smaller joints. Bend at your knees, keep your child close to your body, and avoid twisting. Consider using equipment like a high-standing cot or a supportive baby carrier.

faqs.q: What are some energy-saving tips for busy parents with arthritis?
faqs.a: Batch-cook meals when you have more energy, use online grocery shopping, and create designated play areas to reduce fetching and carrying. Maximise rest periods during your child's naps, and don't be afraid to ask for help with household chores.

faqs.q: Is it safe to use a baby carrier or sling if I have arthritis?
faqs.a: Many parents find carriers and slings helpful, but choose one that distributes weight evenly across your body, such as a soft-structured carrier or a wrap. Ensure it feels comfortable and doesn't strain your joints. A physiotherapist can offer advice on the best type for your specific needs.

faqs.q: Can I apply for PIP if I'm still working?
faqs.a: Yes, absolutely. Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is not means-tested and is not affected by whether you are working or receiving other benefits. The assessment focuses on how your health condition or disability affects your daily life and mobility, not your employment status.

faqs.q: How often do I need to be affected by my arthritis to qualify?
faqs.a: For PIP, your difficulties must have lasted for at least three months and be expected to continue for at least another nine months. This means you don't have to be affected every single day, but the pattern of your symptoms and their impact must be consistent over time. It's important to describe both your good days and your bad days.

faqs.q: What kind of evidence can I use to support my application?
faqs.a: You can provide various types of evidence beyond your application form. This includes letters from your doctor or rheumatologist, prescription lists, records from occupational therapists or physiotherapists, and even a symptom diary that details your difficulties over time. The more evidence you can provide, the stronger your application will be.

Non-pharmacological strategies like gentle exercise, nutrition, and stress management are also important for well-being.

faqs.q: Can I still breastfeed if I have arthritis and take medication?
faqs.a: Many medications for arthritis are considered safe during breastfeeding, but others are not. It's really important to have an open discussion with your rheumatologist and GP about your breastfeeding plans so they can advise on the safest options for you and your baby.

faqs.q: How will pregnancy affect my arthritis symptoms?
faqs.a: The effect of pregnancy on arthritis symptoms varies greatly from person to person. Some people find their symptoms improve during pregnancy, particularly in the second and third trimesters, while others experience no change or even a worsening of symptoms. Your rheumatologist will monitor your condition closely.

faqs.q: What specialist support is available during pregnancy for people with arthritis?
faqs.a: You should expect to receive care from a multi-disciplinary team, including your rheumatologist, obstetrician, and specialist nurses. They will work together to manage your arthritis and pregnancy, providing tailored advice and monitoring throughout.

This can lead to improved physical function and a quicker return to normal activities. Gentle, regular activity like walking, cycling, or swimming is often recommended to strengthen muscles and prepare the body for surgery.

faqs.q: What kind of exercise is best before surgery?
faqs.a: The best exercise is usually a mix of strengthening and light aerobic activity that you can manage comfortably. Walking, cycling, swimming, and gentle exercises prescribed by a physiotherapist are often suitable. Always discuss specifics with your clinical team.

faqs.q: How soon before surgery should I start exercising?
faqs.a: Ideally, you should start as soon as you know you're having surgery. Even a few weeks of consistent, appropriate activity can make a positive difference. The longer you can prepare, the better the potential benefits.

faqs.q: Can I still exercise if I have arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, absolutely. Gentle, consistent movement is often beneficial for arthritis. Your clinical team or physiotherapist can guide you on safe and effective exercises that won't aggravate your condition but will help prepare your body for surgery.

faqs.q: What exactly is a prescription prepayment certificate (PPC)?
faqs.a: A PPC is essentially a season ticket for your prescriptions. You pay a set amount upfront for either three months or twelve months, and then all your prescriptions within that period are free, no matter how many you get.

faqs.q: How do I apply for a prescription prepayment certificate?
faqs.a: You can usually apply for a PPC online through the official government service, over the phone, or by completing a form at a pharmacy. You'll need some personal details and a way to pay.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund if I buy a PPC but then become eligible for free prescriptions?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. If your circumstances change and you become eligible for free prescriptions (for instance, if you turn 60 or start receiving certain benefits), you might be able to claim a refund for any unused full months on your PPC.

faqs.q: Can I get a definitive diagnosis quickly through private care?
faqs.a: Private care can often speed up the diagnostic process by reducing waiting times for specialist appointments and imaging scans. However, the complexity of diagnosing some forms of arthritis means that even privately, it might take a few visits and tests to get a clear picture.

faqs.q: Is private rheumatology a one-off cost, or are there ongoing fees?
faqs.a: Typically, private rheumatology involves ongoing costs. You'll likely pay for initial consultations, follow-up appointments, diagnostic tests (like x-rays or blood tests), and potentially for any procedures or treatments administered privately. Some private health insurance plans may cover these, but it's essential to check your policy.

faqs.q: Will private treatment affect my ability to access care later?
faqs.a: Choosing private treatment for a period does not typically affect your right to access services later on. You can usually move between private and public healthcare pathways if your circumstances change or if your treatment requires a different setting. Discuss any such plans with your doctors to ensure continuity of care.

/blog/reasonable-adjustments-that-actual.answer: Reasonable adjustments for arthritis work best when tailored to your symptoms and job, combining ergonomic equipment, task changes, flexible hours or home working, and a supportive workplace. The article advises early, open communication with employers, regular review as needs change, symptom tracking, and clinician input, especially for new swelling, worsening pain, reduced function, poor sleep, mood changes or stress.

faqs.q: What kind of documentation do I need to request reasonable adjustments?
faqs.a: Often, a letter or report from your general practitioner or specialist outlining your condition and its impact on your work tasks is sufficient. This helps your employer understand your needs and the rationale behind your request.

faqs.q: Can my employer refuse a request for reasonable adjustments?
faqs.a: Employers are generally expected to make 'reasonable' adjustments. They can only refuse if an adjustment is deemed unreasonable due to factors like cost, practicality, or business impact. However, they should always explore alternatives with you.

faqs.q: How often should I review my reasonable adjustments?
faqs.a: It's a good idea to review your adjustments regularly, perhaps annually, or whenever there's a significant change in your symptoms or job role. Your needs can change over time, and adjustments that worked initially might need updating.

/blog/school-run-survival-for-parents-wi.answer: Managing arthritis during the school run requires a multi-faceted approach. Consistent evidence suggests combining appropriate medication with lifestyle adjustments, like gentle, regular movement and stress reduction. Prioritise planning by preparing tasks the night before, and listen to your body, adjusting activity levels rather than pushing through pain. faqs.q: How can I make mornings less rushed and stressful with arthritis?
faqs.a: Planning is key. Lay out clothes, pack lunchboxes, and organise school bags the night before. Consider having a designated 'morning station' for keys, permission slips, and anything else needed for the school run to minimise frantic searching.

faqs.q: What are some gentle exercises to do in the morning to ease stiffness?
faqs.a: Simple range-of-motion exercises can be very helpful. Try gentle neck rotations, shoulder rolls, wrist circles, and ankle pumps while still in bed or preparing for the day. Listen to your body and move within a comfortable range.

faqs.q: My child often needs something at the last minute; how can I manage this without adding strain?
faqs.a: Encourage your child to take more responsibility for their items by creating checklists for them. If something is truly last-minute, try to delegate to another adult if possible, or adapt your movement to protect your joints, perhaps by using a trolley for heavy items.

/blog/should-you-tell-your-employer-abou.answer: The article says telling your employer about arthritis can help if done early and met with understanding, because supportive disclosure may improve job retention, reduce symptom interference and enable reasonable adjustments. It advises discussing concerns with your GP or rheumatologist, tracking symptoms, preparing clear work-related requests, knowing your rights, and seeking help if symptoms worsen.
/blog/should-you-tell-your-employer-abou.breadcrumb: Should You Tell Your Employer About Your Arthritis?

faqs.q: Will telling my employer about my arthritis affect my career progression?
faqs.a: Legally, your employer cannot discriminate against you because of a long-term condition like arthritis. In fact, declaring your condition can allow your employer to make reasonable adjustments that support your work performance and retention, potentially enhancing your career rather than hindering it.

faqs.q: Do I have to tell my employer everything about my medical condition?
faqs.a: You only need to share information that is relevant to your ability to do your job and any reasonable adjustments you might need. You do not have to disclose every detail of your medical history or treatment if it is not pertinent to your work.

faqs.q: What if my employer doesn't offer the adjustments I need?
faqs.a: If discussions with your employer don't lead to satisfactory reasonable adjustments, you can seek advice from an occupational health specialist, a trade union representative, or an employment advisor. There are resources available to help mediate these conversations and ensure your rights are upheld.

/blog/shoulder-arthroscopy-and-arthritis.title: Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fi | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/shoulder-arthroscopy-and-arthritis.description: Useful for some impingement; less so for advanced arthritis. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's clinical team — practical, plain-English...
/blog/shoulder-arthroscopy-and-arthritis.question: Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fi
/blog/shoulder-arthroscopy-and-arthritis.answer: Shoulder arthroscopy will not cure arthritis or reverse joint damage. Evidence shows short-term benefits for some impingement, but it is not significantly better than non-surgical approaches long-term. For moderate to severe arthritis, arthroscopy offers little lasting benefit. It is typically reserved for specific situations when conservative methods like physical therapy, medication, and injections have failed.
/blog/shoulder-arthroscopy-and-arthritis.breadcrumb: Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fi

faqs.q: Will shoulder arthroscopy cure my arthritis?
faqs.a: No, shoulder arthroscopy typically will not cure arthritis. For certain types of arthritis, it might help manage specific symptoms like impingement or remove loose fragments of cartilage, but it doesn't reverse joint damage or prevent further progression of the disease.

faqs.q: How long does recovery from shoulder arthroscopy take?
faqs.a: Recovery times vary highly depending on the extent of the procedure and individual healing. Generally, it can take several weeks to a few months of guided physical therapy to regain strength and movement, with full recovery sometimes taking up to six months or longer.

faqs.q: What are the alternatives to shoulder arthroscopy for arthritis?
faqs.a: Alternatives include a comprehensive physical therapy programme, pain relief medication, steroid injections into the joint, lifestyle adjustments, and, in some severe cases, open surgery such as a shoulder replacement for extensive joint damage.

/blog/shoulder-pain-reaching-ra-vs-oa.title: Shoulder Pain When Reaching: RA vs OA Differences | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/shoulder-pain-reaching-ra-vs-oa.description: RA tends to swell both shoulders symmetrically and worsens with rest; OA usually affects one shoulder and worsens with use. Telling them apart.
/blog/shoulder-pain-reaching-ra-vs-oa.question: Shoulder Pain When Reaching: RA vs OA Differences
/blog/shoulder-pain-reaching-ra-vs-oa.answer: Inflammatory arthritis typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis, such as osteoarthritis, generally worsens with prolonged use. Recommended approaches include 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold applications, and good sleep hygiene. Seek medical advice for sudden hot, red, swollen joints, unexplained weight loss, morning stiffness over an hour for two weeks, or new numbness or weakness.

/blog/steroid-injections-vs-oral-steroid.question: Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense
/blog/steroid-injections-vs-oral-steroid.answer: Steroid injections typically alleviate pain and inflammation in specific joints for several weeks to months, often taking a few days to a week to become effective. Oral steroids are generally used for widespread inflammation. Neither is a long-term solution, and both carry risks with overuse. They should be part of a broader management strategy including exercise, therapy, and weight management.
/blog/steroid-injections-vs-oral-steroid.breadcrumb: Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense

faqs.q: How long do steroid injections take to work?
faqs.a: Typically, you might start to feel the effects of a steroid injection within a few days, though for some, it can take up to a week. The full pain relief can then last from several weeks to a few months, depending on the individual and the joint injected.

faqs.q: Can I have multiple steroid injections?
faqs.a: Yes, it's possible to have multiple steroid injections, but your clinician will carefully consider the frequency and number. Too many injections into the same joint can, over time, weaken surrounding tissues, so there are usually limits on how often and how many you can receive.

faqs.q: Are there alternatives to steroids for arthritis flare-ups?
faqs.a: Absolutely. Depending on the type and severity of your arthritis, alternatives might include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), other pain relief medications, physical therapy, heat or cold packs, and various topical treatments. Your clinician can discuss the best options for your specific situation.

/blog/stopping-arthritis-medication-safe.title: Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/stopping-arthritis-medication-safe.description: Remission feels great — but stopping too quickly risks a flare. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's clinical team — practical, plain-Engli...
/blog/stopping-arthritis-medication-safe.question: Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide
/blog/stopping-arthritis-medication-safe.answer: Stopping arthritis medication should always be a joint decision with your rheumatologist, even if you feel well. Abruptly stopping or significantly reducing effective treatments for inflammatory arthritis can increase flare-up risk and potential joint damage. It is a gradual process, often taking months, with consistent symptom monitoring throughout. If symptoms return, contact your care team promptly.
/blog/stopping-arthritis-medication-safe.breadcrumb: Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide

faqs.q: Can I stop my medication if I feel completely well?
faqs.a: Even if you feel completely well, stopping medication should always be a joint decision with your rheumatologist. "Feeling well" can sometimes mask underlying disease activity, and stopping too soon can lead to a flare.

faqs.q: How long does it take to safely reduce medication?
faqs.a: The timeframe for safely reducing medication varies greatly depending on your individual condition, the type of medication, and how long you've been in remission. It's often a gradual process that can take months, overseen by your care team.

faqs.q: What should I do if my symptoms return after reducing medication?
faqs.a: If your symptoms return or worsen after reducing medication, contact your rheumatology team or GP promptly. They may advise restarting your previous dose or adjusting your treatment plan to bring your condition back under control.

/blog/strength-training-on-biologics-is-.title: Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe? | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/strength-training-on-biologics-is-.description: Resistance work is not only safe — it's recommended. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's clinical team — practical, plain-English advice.
/blog/strength-training-on-biologics-is-.question: Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?
/blog/strength-training-on-biologics-is-.answer: Strength training is generally safe and recommended for people with arthritis, even those on biologics. Research shows it can improve muscle strength, reduce pain, and boost physical function. It's crucial to start slowly, focus on proper form, and listen to your body, stopping if you experience new or lasting joint pain. Always discuss your exercise plan with your clinician.
/blog/strength-training-on-biologics-is-.breadcrumb: Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?

faqs.q: Will strength training make my arthritis worse?
faqs.a: No, when done correctly and tailored to your condition, strength training is highly unlikely to worsen your arthritis. In fact, it can protect your joints by strengthening the muscles around them, improving stability and reducing impact during daily activities. Listening to your body and working with a professional are key to a safe and effective programme.

faqs.q: How soon after starting biologics can I begin strength training?
faqs.a: It's generally safe to continue or start strength training once your condition is stable and you're tolerating your biologic medication well. However, always discuss this with your rheumatologist or specialist nurse. They can advise based on your specific health situation and how your body is responding to treatment.

faqs.q: What if I have a flare-up while strength training?
faqs.a: During an arthritis flare-up, it's wise to reduce the intensity and type of exercise. You might switch to gentler activities like walking or stretching, or rest the affected joints. Once the flare-up subsides, you can gradually return to your strength training routine. Always consult your clinician if you're unsure or if the flare-up is severe.

/blog/supporting-a-partner-with-arthriti.answer: The post says partners can support someone with arthritis through small daily acts, open communication and practical help with joint-straining tasks. faqs.q: How can I explain my arthritis pain to my partner so they truly understand?
faqs.a: Try to use analogies that relate to their experiences, like comparing it to a deep ache after a marathon or constant toothache. Explain how it affects simple daily tasks and how it can fluctuate, even hourly. Being open and honest about your feelings, rather than just the physical pain, can also help them empathise.

faqs.q: What are some simple ways my partner can help me around the house without making me feel helpless?
faqs.a: Your partner can help by taking on tasks that put strain on your joints, such as lifting heavy items, opening stubborn jars, or reaching high shelves. They could also help prepare meals or assist with household chores during a flare. The key is to communicate what you need without feeling like a burden, and to appreciate their efforts.

faqs.q: Is it OK to have sex when I have arthritis pain?
faqs.a: Intimacy is important for relationships, and arthritis doesn't mean you have to stop. Communicate openly with your partner about what feels comfortable and what doesn't. You might find certain positions or times of day are better, perhaps after medication or a warm bath. Experimenting together and focusing on closeness can help maintain intimacy.

faqs.q: How do I explain "pain" to a young child?
faqs.a: You can describe pain using words they understand, like "my joints feel a bit stiff today, like an old rusty robot" or "sometimes my hands feel like they have a little ouchie." Focus on what it means for you, rather than the scary aspects, such as "it makes it harder for me to carry you sometimes, but I still love cuddles."

faqs.q: What if my child gets upset or scared?
faqs.a: It's natural for children to react emotionally. Reassure them that you are taking care of yourself and that they are safe. Listen to their fears without judgment and validate their feelings. You might say, "I understand why that makes you sad, and it's okay to feel that way. We'll get through this together."

faqs.q: Should I involve my child in my treatment?
faqs.a: You can involve them in small, appropriate ways that empower them, such as asking them to fetch a heat pack, or letting them choose a quiet activity to do with you when you're feeling low. This gives them a sense of contribution and understanding without burdening them with responsibility for your condition.

/blog/tapering-biologics-what-the-latest.title: Tapering Biologics: What the Latest Trials Show | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/tapering-biologics-what-the-latest.description: Dose-reduction studies suggest many patients can step down safely. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's clinical team — practical, plain-En...
/blog/tapering-biologics-what-the-latest.question: Tapering Biologics: What the Latest Trials Show
/blog/tapering-biologics-what-the-latest.answer: For people with well-controlled inflammatory arthritis, reviews of randomised trials show that a gradual reduction in biologic medication dosage can be considered. This involves spacing out injections or reducing the dose while maintaining disease control. Any tapering strategy should be highly individualised, carefully monitored, and undertaken in close consultation with a specialist to balance disease control with reduced side effects and cost.
/blog/tapering-biologics-what-the-latest.breadcrumb: Tapering Biologics: What the Latest Trials Show

faqs.q: Can I stop my biologic if I feel completely well?
faqs.a: Feeling well is a great sign, but it doesn't usually mean your arthritis is cured. Biologics help keep your condition under control, and stopping them completely without a specialist's guidance can lead to a quick return of symptoms. Always talk to your rheumatology team first.

faqs.q: How quickly can I taper my biologic dose?
faqs.a: The pace of tapering is highly individual and very gradual. Your specialist will work with you to establish a step-by-step plan, often involving small reductions over several months, with regular monitoring to ensure your disease remains stable. Speeding up the process on your own isn't recommended.

faqs.q: What happens if my symptoms return during tapering?
faqs.a: If your symptoms start to return or worsen during a tapering process, it's really important to contact your rheumatology team straight away. They can assess the situation and usually advise on increasing your dose back to a previous level, or adjusting your treatment plan, to bring your arthritis back under control.

/blog/thumb-base-pain-early-hand-arthrit.question: Thumb Base Pain: Early Signs of Hand Arthritis
/blog/thumb-base-pain-early-hand-arthrit.answer: Thumb base pain can indicate early hand arthritis, which may be inflammatory or degenerative. Inflammatory arthritis often improves with movement, while degenerative arthritis can worsen with prolonged use. Effective management includes 150 minutes of weekly moderate exercise, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, and heat or cold applications. /blog/topical-nsaids-often-overlooked-of.description: Gels and creams deliver pain relief with fewer systemic side effects — especially for knees and hands. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's...
/blog/topical-nsaids-often-overlooked-of.question: Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective
/blog/topical-nsaids-often-overlooked-of.answer: Topical anti-inflammatory gels and creams can be effective for joint pain, particularly in hands and knees. They deliver pain relief locally with fewer systemic side effects than oral medications. Use them regularly, 2-3 times daily, applying enough product as advised in the leaflet. Avoid use on broken skin, and consult a doctor if pain worsens or new symptoms appear.
/blog/topical-nsaids-often-overlooked-of.breadcrumb: Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective

faqs.q: Can I use these gels and creams long-term?
faqs.a: For most people, topical anti-inflammatory gels and creams can be used long-term as directed, especially for managing chronic joint pain. However, it's always best to discuss ongoing use with your doctor, particularly if you have other health conditions or are taking other medications.

faqs.q: Do topical pain relievers interact with other medications?
faqs.a: Because very little of the medication gets into your bloodstream when applied topically, interactions with other medications are much less common than with oral tablets. Still, if you're taking blood thinners or have kidney problems, it's wise to check with your doctor or pharmacist.

faqs.q: How quickly should I expect to feel better?
faqs.a: You might start to feel some pain relief within minutes or hours of application, but it can take a few days of regular use to experience the full benefit. If you don't notice any improvement after a week of consistent use, it's a good idea to speak to a healthcare professional.

/blog/total-knee-replacement-a-uk-patien.title: Total Knee Replacement: A UK Patient's Guide for 2026 | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/total-knee-replacement-a-uk-patien.description: From referral to recovery — what to expect at each stage. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's clinical team — practical, plain-English adv...
/blog/total-knee-replacement-a-uk-patien.question: Total Knee Replacement: A UK Patient's Guide for 2026
/blog/total-knee-replacement-a-uk-patien.answer: For many, non-surgical methods effectively manage knee pain. Tailored exercise, weight management, and pain relief consistently delay or avoid surgery. A 'stepped care' approach recommends starting with less invasive treatments, progressing only if needed. Patient satisfaction after knee replacement is highest when non-surgical options are explored and individuals are prepared.
/blog/total-knee-replacement-a-uk-patien.breadcrumb: Total Knee Replacement: A UK Patient's Guide for 2026

faqs.q: How long does a knee replacement typically last?
faqs.a: Most modern total knee replacements are designed to last for 15 to 20 years, and often longer. The longevity can be influenced by factors such as a person's activity levels, weight, and overall health. Regular follow-ups with your orthopaedic team can help monitor its condition.

faqs.q: Can I still be active after a knee replacement?
faqs.a: Yes, most people can return to many activities they enjoyed before surgery, often with less pain. Low-impact activities like walking, swimming, cycling, and even golf are generally encouraged. High-impact sports like running or aggressive jumping should typically be avoided to protect the new joint.

faqs.q: What is the recovery time like after knee replacement surgery?
faqs.a: Initial recovery often involves spending a few days in hospital, followed by several weeks of physiotherapy at home or an outpatient clinic. Most people can resume driving after about 4-6 weeks and more day-to-day activities within 3 months, though full recovery and strength building can take up to a year.

/blog/universal-credit-and-arthritis-lim.answer: The post explains how people with arthritis can prepare for a Universal Credit Work Capability Assessment by giving an honest picture of symptoms, including bad days, and bringing medical evidence, therapy notes, medication details and a symptom diary. It highlights personalised clinical, occupational and workplace support, advises prompt clinician contact if symptoms worsen, and notes decisions can be challenged.
/blog/universal-credit-and-arthritis-lim.breadcrumb: Universal Credit and Arthritis: Limited Capability for Work

faqs.q: What kind of information should I bring to my Work Capability Assessment?
faqs.a: It's helpful to bring all relevant medical letters, reports from specialists (like rheumatologists or physiotherapists), a detailed symptom diary covering several weeks, and a list of all current medications, including dosages.

faqs.q: Will my assessor be a medical professional?
faqs.a: Assessors come from a variety of healthcare backgrounds, including nurses, occupational therapists, and physiotherapists. While they are healthcare professionals, they are not usually specialists in your specific condition.

faqs.q: Can I appeal a decision if I disagree with the outcome?
faqs.a: Yes, if you're not happy with the decision, you have the right to challenge it. The first step is usually to ask for a Mandatory Reconsideration, where the decision is reviewed again. If you're still not satisfied, you can then appeal to an independent tribunal.

/blog/university-with-arthritis-disabili.answer: Disabled Students’ Allowance can help students with arthritis access tailored university support, including specialist equipment, non-medical helpers and academic adjustments. The article advises applying early, contacting disability services, tracking symptoms, maintaining gentle movement and self-care, and involving support networks. It also recommends speaking to a GP, physiotherapist or rheumatologist if symptoms worsen or affect study.

faqs.q: Can I get support for more than one health condition?
faqs.a: Yes, the Disabled Students' Allowance (DSA) can cover support for multiple eligible health conditions, including arthritis, if they impact your ability to study. You will typically be assessed for all your conditions simultaneously.

faqs.q: What if my symptoms change during my course?
faqs.a: If your arthritis symptoms worsen or change significantly during your university course, you can request a review of your Disabled Students' Allowance support. Contact your university's disability services team; they can guide you through the process of reappraising your needs.

faqs.q: Does applying for DSA affect my student finance?
faqs.a: No, applying for or receiving the Disabled Students' Allowance does not affect any other student finance you receive, such as student loans or grants. DSA is provided in addition to these and is specifically for costs related to your disability.

/blog/walking-30-minutes-a-day-while-on-.question: Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan
/blog/walking-30-minutes-a-day-while-on-.answer: Walking daily with arthritis is generally safe and recommended, especially when gentle and progressive. Regular, moderate intensity exercise, including walking, improves joint function, reduces pain, and boosts overall quality of life. Tailored activity, alongside medication, helps keep muscles strong and supports heart health. Listen to your body and adjust if experiencing pain; consistency is more important than intensity.
/blog/walking-30-minutes-a-day-while-on-.breadcrumb: Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan

faqs.q: Can walking help reduce the side effects of DMARDs?
faqs.a: Walking itself doesn't directly reduce DMARD side effects. However, regular physical activity can improve overall wellbeing, energy levels, and mood, which can help you cope better with any challenges from your medication. It's important to discuss any medication side effects with your rheumatology team.

faqs.q: How do I know if I'm overdoing it when walking?
faqs.a: A good rule of thumb is that you should still be able to hold a conversation while walking. If you're too breathless to talk, you're likely working too hard. Also, listen to your joints: a little stiffness might be normal, but sharp or increasing pain during or after your walk is a sign to slow down or rest.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk every day with arthritis?
faqs.a: For most people with arthritis, walking every day is not only safe but highly recommended, provided it's gentle and progressive. Consistency is more important than intensity. If you have active inflammation or are experiencing a flare-up, you might need to adjust your routine and walk for shorter periods or on alternate days.

/blog/weight-management-arthritis-eviden.question: Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence
/blog/weight-management-arthritis-eviden.answer: Weight management is an effective strategy for managing arthritis symptoms. A 5% reduction in body weight can significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis symptoms. A 10% reduction in weight can even produce benefits comparable to some medications. This is achieved through consistent, small changes, tracking outcomes like pain on waking, longest pain-free intervals, and functional improvements.

/blog/what-sustained-remission-means-in-.question: What Sustained Remission Means in RA
/blog/what-sustained-remission-means-in-.answer: Sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis means stable minimal or no disease activity, not a cure. The article says it is a key treatment goal, often maintained through ongoing medication, monitoring, gentle regular movement and lifestyle support. It advises personalised clinician guidance, symptom tracking, pacing activity, and prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid function loss or medication side effects.
/blog/what-sustained-remission-means-in-.breadcrumb: What Sustained Remission Means in RA

faqs.q: Can I reduce my medication once I'm in sustained remission?
faqs.a: Sometimes, yes, but this must be done very carefully and under the guidance of your rheumatologist. Reducing medication needs to be a shared decision, considering your individual circumstances and risk of flare.

faqs.q: How is 'sustained remission' actually measured?
faqs.a: It's measured using a combination of factors, including your own report of symptoms (like how much pain or stiffness you have), your doctor's examination of your joints, and blood tests to check for inflammation markers. This data is often fed into a specific scoring system.

faqs.q: Does being in remission mean I can stop exercising?
faqs.a: No, regular exercise remains very important. It helps maintain joint flexibility, muscle strength, and overall well-being, even when you're feeling good. Your specialist or a physiotherapist can advise on suitable activities.

/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-.title: Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-.description: Strength training improves drug efficacy by reducing systemic inflammation. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's clinical team — practical...
/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-.question: Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better
/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-.answer: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function, and enhancing quality of life. This integrated approach, which combines medication with movement, is recommended in clinical guidelines. Exercise is thought to lower widespread inflammation, maintain healthy weight, strengthen muscles, and improve mood, all of which support treatment response.
/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-.breadcrumb: Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better

faqs.q: Does gentle movement count, or do I need to do intense workouts?
faqs.a: Yes, gentle movement absolutely counts! Activities like walking, swimming, or tai chi can be very effective. The key is consistency and finding activities you enjoy that don't aggravate your joints. Intense workouts are generally not recommended for most people with arthritis.

faqs.q: How soon will I notice a difference in how my medication works?
faqs.a: It can take time to notice the full benefits of combining exercise with your medication. Most people find improvements gradually over several weeks or months. Keeping a symptom diary can help you track these changes and discuss them with your healthcare team.

faqs.q: Can exercise replace my arthritis medication entirely?
faqs.a: For most types of arthritis, exercise is a complementary treatment, not a replacement for medication. Your medicines work in specific ways to manage the underlying disease. Exercise helps reduce symptoms, improve function, and support your overall health alongside your prescribed treatment plan.

/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthrit.title: Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010 | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthrit.description: Reasonable adjustments are a legal entitlement, not a favour. Evidence-based UK guide from Living With Arthritis's clinical team — practical, plain-English...
/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthrit.question: Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010
/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthrit.answer: Arthritis can impact work performance due to its effects on physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. Many individuals with arthritis work successfully, often with workplace adjustments. Reasonable adjustments, which are a legal entitlement, include flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, and adjusted duties. You do not have to disclose your arthritis to your employer unless it poses a health and safety risk.
/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthrit.breadcrumb: Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010

faqs.q: Can arthritis affect my ability to do my job?
faqs.a: Yes, arthritis can impact various aspects of your work, including physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. However, many people with arthritis work successfully, often with the help of adjustments and support.

faqs.q: What kind of "reasonable adjustments" can I ask for at work?
faqs.a: Reasonable adjustments are changes that help you do your job effectively. Examples include flexible working hours, ergonomic equipment (like a special chair or keyboard), adjusted duties, or even a change of workstation.

faqs.q: Do I have to tell my employer I have arthritis?
faqs.a: You are not legally obliged to disclose your arthritis unless it poses a health and safety risk. However, telling your employer can help them understand your needs and allow you to request reasonable adjustments.

/blog/juvenile-arthritis-uk.answer: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a group of autoimmune conditions causing joint inflammation in children under 16, affecting approximately 15,000 children and young people in the UK. Parents might notice limping, morning stiffness, swollen joints, or unusual irritability. Diagnosis involves clinical assessment by a paediatric rheumatologist. Treatment aims for remission, using medicines like NSAIDs, methotrexate, and biologics, alongside physiotherapy to maintain joint function and strength.

For big toe arthritis, you might notice difficulty walking and a bony bump. Ankle arthritis often causes deep pain, stiffness in the morning, and swelling.
